title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, & ggplot2
text:
Key Concepts
A ggplot has three basic parts:

Data — the table being plotted
Aesthetics — variables mapped to things like x, y, and color with aes()
Geoms — the marks drawn on the graph, such as points, lines, or bars

Use + to add layers to a plot. For example, geom_point() makes a scatterplot, while geom_histogram() shows the distribution of one numeric variable.
A variable goes inside aes() if its values control the plot’s appearance: aes(color = reliability). A fixed color goes outside aes(): color = "steelblue".
ACS estimates have margins of error (MOEs). A large MOE means I should be careful when comparing estimates, especially for small areas.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Key Concepts
R code can save a result in an object:
result <- filter(counties, population > 50000) result is the object that stores the output. <- is the assignment arrow. filter() is a function, also called a verb in dplyr. counties is the input data. population > 50000 is an argument. Anything after # is a comment and does not run.
The ACS is a survey of roughly 3% of U.S. households. It produces an estimate and a margin of error (MOE). The 1-year ACS is more current but only covers places with populations above 65,000, while the 5-year ACS covers smaller geographies such as tracts and block groups.
A GEOID is an identifier stored as text so it keeps leading zeros. For example, Pennsylvania GEOIDs begin with 42. Census data can be in:
Long/tidy format: one row for each geography-variable combination. Wide format: one row per geography, with each variable in a separate column.
Wide format is useful when I need to compare variables, such as population and income, side by side.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at the median gross rent across counties in North Carolina, and ask which communities are measured most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:

my_state <- "NC"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B25064_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

section: How big is the margin of error?

How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                             myvarE myvarM   popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                             <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 37001 Alamance County, North Carolina    1007     28 174286    NA
2 37003 Alexander County, North Carolina    745     36  36440    NA
3 37005 Alleghany County, North Carolina    755    114  11075    NA
4 37007 Anson County, North Carolina        849     63  21903    NA
5 37009 Ashe County, North Carolina         774     39  26831    NA
6 37011 Avery County, North Carolina        791     68  17643    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         51        173508.
2 Low confidence           8         11434.
3 Moderate                41         40097.


High-confidence counties have an average population of about 173,508 people, while low-confidence counties average about 11,434 people. Moderate-confidence counties average about 40,097 people. This shows a clear pattern: smaller counties tend to have less reliable ACS median gross-rent estimates.
Reflection: The ACS estimates of median gross rent are least reliable in several small North Carolina counties, especially Chowan, Gates, Graham, Hyde, Cherokee, Washington, and Tyrrell Counties. Chowan County has the largest relative margin of error: its estimated median gross rent is $766, with a margin of error of $290, or 37.9%. This means the published estimate has a large amount of uncertainty and should not be treated as a precise measure of what renters pay there. Gates and Graham Counties also have very high relative margins of error, at 22.8% and 21.5%, respectively.
This pattern occurs because the ACS is based on a sample rather than a complete count of every household. Smaller counties have fewer households in the survey sample, so their estimates are less stable and have larger margins of error. In contrast, counties with larger populations generally have more survey responses and therefore more reliable estimates. My results show that 51 North Carolina counties have high-confidence estimates, while 13 counties fall into the low-confidence category.
If a state agency allocated housing-assistance funding based only on these median-rent estimates, without considering their margins of error, it could make unfair decisions. Small counties with uncertain estimates could receive too little funding if their rent is underestimated, or funds could be directed inefficiently if rent is overestimated. Residents of rural counties, where housing data are already limited, would be most likely to be affected. Policymakers should therefore use ACS estimates together with their margins of error and avoid treating all county-level numbers as equally certain.

We also introduced sf functions for finding tracts near stations and measuring spatial relationships.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, & Coordinate Systems
text:
Key Concepts
A GEOID identifies a Census geography. It should be stored as text so leading zeros are preserved. When joining two tables, the GEOID columns need to refer to the same type of geography and use matching values.
A left_join() keeps every row from the first table and adds matching columns from the second. If a GEOID has no match, the new column contains NA. When the first table is an sf object, its geometry column stays attached.
sf stands for simple features. An sf table contains ordinary columns plus a geometry column with shapes such as points or polygons.
A CRS tells R how coordinates relate to places on Earth:

CRS
Units




4326
WGS 84
Degrees

NAD 83
Degrees

Pennsylvania South State Plane

5070
NAD 83 / Conus Albers

A geographic CRS uses longitude and latitude. A projected CRS represents locations on a flat map, often in feet or meters. Projections involve tradeoffs: one may preserve local shapes, while another preserves areas or distances better for a particular purpose.
Use st_crs() to check a layer’s CRS. st_set_crs() assigns the correct existing CRS label when it is missing; it does not move coordinates. st_transform() converts coordinates into another CRS. I need to check the units before making a buffer or interpreting a distance.
Some useful spatial functions are:

st_buffer() creates an area around a feature.
st_filter() selects features with a spatial relationship, such as tracts that intersect station buffers.
st_intersection() creates the shared geometry where features overlap.
st_union() combines geometries into one shape.
st_join() adds attributes based on a spatial relationship.
st_distance() calculates distances between features.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, & Coordinate Systems
text:
Proving R Works
This example joins income data from two years by GEOID. The 2023 table goes first, so all three of its GEOIDs remain. GEOID "300" has no 2015 match and receives NA.

library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

income_23 <- tibble(
  GEOID = c("100", "200", "300"),
  med_inc_23 = c(82000, 31500, 45000)
)

income_15 <- tibble(
  GEOID = c("100", "200", "400"),
  med_inc_15 = c(61000, 27000, 39000)
)

income_joined <- left_join(income_23, income_15, by = "GEOID")

income_joined

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  GEOID med_inc_23 med_inc_15
  <chr>      <dbl>      <dbl>
1 100        82000      61000
2 200        31500      27000
3 300        45000         NA


I can check the join by counting rows and missing values:

income_joined |>
  summarize(
    rows = n(),
    missing_2015_income = sum(is.na(med_inc_15))
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
   rows missing_2015_income
  <int>               <int>
1     3                   1


The result should show 3 rows and 1 missing 2015 income value. This example uses ordinary tables; a spatial version would also have a geometry column.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, & Coordinate Systems
text:
Reflection
I learned that joining Census data to a map depends on both the table key and the spatial data. A join can run successfully while still leaving unmatched GEOIDs, so I should check the row count and missing values afterward. I also understand why I need to check the CRS before making a half-mile buffer: the number supplied to st_buffer() only makes sense when I know the layer’s distance units.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 1: Reconstructing the Article’s Data
The article compares Philadelphia neighborhood poverty using the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS 5-year estimates. I use survey = "acs5" with year = 2010 and year = 2017 to retrieve those periods. The periods do not overlap, so they do not share collection years. For the change test, I use the standard approximation that the estimates from the two periods are independent.
I use table B17001: B17001_002 counts people below the poverty level, and B17001_001 counts people for whom poverty status is determined. Dividing these gives the poverty rate. I assume this measure corresponds to the article’s overall poverty measure. Because its neighborhood-to-tract definitions are unavailable, I compare Philadelphia census tracts rather than reconstructing its neighborhood totals. I match tracts by GEOID and assume matched tracts represent comparable areas; matching identifiers alone does not verify unchanged boundaries.

What the results show
Of the 376 tracts included in the comparison, 36 showed a statistically detectable increase in poverty and 27 showed a detectable decrease at 90% confidence. The remaining 313 tracts, or 83.2%, showed no statistically detectable change. This does not mean their poverty rates stayed exactly the same. It means the estimated changes were not large enough relative to their uncertainty to distinguish them from zero.
The reliability table also shows that most tract poverty rates were only somewhat reliable. In 2006–2010, 11 tracts were classified as reliable, 321 as somewhat reliable, and 44 as unreliable. In 2013–2017, those counts were 22, 332, and 22. These categories describe the precision of each period’s poverty rate; they do not directly determine whether the change between periods is statistically detectable.
Overall, the results show increases in some tracts and decreases in others. They do not establish what happened in the specific neighborhoods named in the article, because the article’s neighborhood-to-tract definitions are unavailable. The tract counts also do not measure the change in Philadelphia’s overall poverty rate, since tracts contain different numbers of people.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
section: Part 3: Which Claims Does the Evidence Support?
text:
Part 3: Which Claims Does the Evidence Support?
Supported: The article reports that poverty increased in some parts of Philadelphia. My tract-level analysis supports that broad pattern: 36 tracts showed statistically detectable increases between 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. However, 27 tracts showed detectable decreases, so the direction of change varied across the city. Not supported by this analysis: Treating every estimated increase as clear evidence that conditions worsened would overstate the findings. For example, Tract 9891 had an estimated increase of 23.3 percentage points, but its extremely large margin of error prevents a confident conclusion about the direction of change. Across all 376 comparable tracts, 313 changes were not statistically distinguishable from zero. This does not prove that poverty was unchanged in those places.
Cannot be determined: I cannot verify the article’s claim that Eastwick’s poverty rate rose from 12% to 26%, or that it had the largest neighborhood increase, because the article does not identify the tracts used to define each neighborhood. The same limitation prevents verification of Fairhill’s reported 61% poverty rate. My analysis also does not test the article’s claim about increasing poverty among white residents: the variables used here describe poverty across the full poverty-status population, not a specific racial group. Finally, these comparisons cannot establish the suggested causes of change, such as opioid use or migration. Those explanations would require additional evidence.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 4: A More Defensible Account
Philadelphia’s poverty trends varied across census tracts between the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 American Community Survey periods. Among 376 tracts with usable poverty rates in both periods, 36 showed increases and 27 showed decreases that were statistically detectable at 90% confidence. For the other 313, uncertainty was too large to establish a change. These results indicate worsening poverty in some areas and improvement in others, rather than a uniform trend. They also show why a large estimated increase should not automatically be treated as a clear deterioration. The article’s exact figures for neighborhoods such as Eastwick and Fairhill cannot be verified through this tract-level analysis without knowing how the neighborhood boundaries were defined.

title: Week 5: Linear Regression for Prediction
text:
Key Concepts

Outcomes, predictors, and noise
A statistical model can be written as:
\[
Y = f(X) + \varepsilon
\]

\(Y\) is the outcome we want to explain or predict, such as median rent.
\(X\) contains the predictors, such as income or educational attainment.
\(f(X)\) is the relationship the model tries to learn.
\(\varepsilon\) represents everything affecting rent that is not captured by the model, including random noise and omitted characteristics.

For a simple linear regression:
\[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1X + \varepsilon
\]
The fitted prediction is:
\[
\hat{Y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1X
\]
The intercept, \(\hat{\beta}_0\), is the predicted outcome when the predictor equals zero. The slope, \(\hat{\beta}_1\), describes the predicted change in the outcome associated with a one-unit increase in the predictor.


Prediction and inference
Regression output can be read in two different ways:

Inference focuses on \(\hat{\beta}\) and asks how a predictor is associated with the outcome.
Prediction focuses on \(\hat{Y}\) and asks how accurately the model can predict an outcome for observations it has not seen.

A coefficient can help prediction without proving causation. For example, the number of Indego stations may help predict rent, but the model cannot prove that adding a station causes rent to increase. Station locations may represent other neighborhood characteristics that the model does not include.


Fitting a linear model in R
A simple rent model can be fitted with:
m1 <- lm(med_rent ~ med_inc, data = tracts)
summary(m1)
The formula can be read as: predict med_rent using med_inc.
In our class example, the estimated income coefficient was approximately 0.0081. This represents about $0.0081 in additional predicted monthly rent for each additional dollar of annual household income. Multiplying by $10,000 makes the result easier to understand:
\[
0.0081 \times 10{,}000 = 81
\]
A tract with $10,000 more in median household income therefore had a predicted monthly rent approximately $81 higher.
A small p-value provides evidence that an association is statistically detectable. It does not tell us whether the effect is large, whether it is causal, or whether the model predicts new observations well.


Least squares and residuals
Linear regression chooses the line that minimizes the sum of squared errors:
\[
\sum (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2
\]
A residual is the difference between an observed value and its prediction:
\[
e_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i
\]

A positive residual means the actual rent is higher than predicted.
A negative residual means the actual rent is lower than predicted.
A residual near zero means the prediction is close to the observed rent.

Mapping residuals can reveal spatial patterns. If nearby tracts have similar residuals, the model may be missing a location-based characteristic.


Rigid and flexible models
Models can be arranged from more rigid to more flexible:



More rigid
Middle
More flexible




Linear regression
Lasso and ridge
Trees


Logistic regression
Random forest
Boosting and neural networks



Rigid models are usually easier to explain and interpret. Flexible models can capture more complicated relationships, but they can be harder to understand and may overfit the training data.
A parametric model, such as linear regression, assumes a particular functional form and estimates a fixed set of parameters. A nonparametric model makes fewer assumptions about the functional form and can follow more complicated patterns in the data.


Model fit versus prediction
\(R^2\) measures how much of the variation in the outcome is explained by the model in the data used to fit it. A higher \(R^2\) indicates a better in-sample fit, but it does not guarantee better predictions for new data.
A train/test split separates the observations into two groups:

The training set is used to fit the model.
The test set is used to evaluate predictions on unseen observations.

In class, we used approximately 80% of the tracts for training and 20% for testing.
Prediction error was measured using root mean squared error:
\[
RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum(Y_i-\hat{Y}_i)^2}
\]
RMSE is expressed in the same units as the outcome. For a rent model, an RMSE of $250 means that predictions miss the observed monthly rent by approximately $250. A lower RMSE is better.


Cross-validation
One train/test split can give different results depending on which observations are selected. K-fold cross-validation provides a more stable evaluation.
For five-fold cross-validation:

Divide the observations into five groups.
Hold out one group as the test set.
Train the model using the other four groups.
Calculate the test RMSE.
Repeat until each group has been used for testing.
Average the five RMSE values.

We used the same folds when comparing models so that the comparison was fair.
This use of CV means cross-validation. It is different from the coefficient of variation, which measures the uncertainty of an ACS estimate.


Regression diagnostics
A good residual plot should look like a random cloud around zero.
Homoscedasticity means the residuals have a similar amount of spread across the range of predicted values. Heteroscedasticity means the spread changes, often creating a funnel shape. In that case, one RMSE may hide the fact that the model makes much larger errors for some observations.
Noise in the outcome \(Y\) becomes part of the residuals. Noise in a predictor \(X\) can flatten the estimated slope.
Multicollinearity occurs when predictors are strongly related to each other. It can make individual coefficients unstable and difficult to interpret. For a prediction task, the main question is whether the variables improve prediction accuracy on unseen data, which can be checked with cross-validation.

Reflection
I learned that fitting the data and predicting new observations are related but different goals. A model can have a higher \(R^2\) because it fits the existing observations better, but cross-validation is needed to determine whether it also predicts unseen tracts better. I also understand that a coefficient describes an association while a residual identifies where the actual outcome differs from the model’s prediction.
Mapping the residuals was especially useful because it showed that model errors may form geographic clusters. If nearby tracts have rents that are consistently higher than predicted, the model may be missing a spatial feature such as access to Center City, universities, transit, newer housing, or other neighborhood amenities.

The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}

text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:

Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)))

summary(tracts$n_burglary)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   9.446  13.000  48.000 


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)

Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.

  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)

Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)

Reading the coefficient: you can’t read either coefficient alone anymore. The effect of X depends on where you are along X. A positive linear term with a negative squared term means Y rises with X and then levels off or turns down. Plot the fitted curve to see it:


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = dist_ch_mi, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  theme_minimal()











5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )

tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(ring)

Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Each coefficient is the difference from the reference: ringOuter is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts compared to core tracts, holding everything else in the model constant. To change the reference, use relevel(ring, ref = "Outer").






NoteCheck your group sizes



If a category has only a handful of tracts, its coefficient is unstable, and in cross-validation some folds may not contain it at all. Aim for at least 20 tracts per category.

Answer: Which transformation helped most? For your categorical variable, write one sentence reading one of its coefficients correctly, naming the reference level.
The squared City Hall distance transformation helped the most, producing the lowest CV RMSE of 9.76, compared with 12.46 for the baseline model. Using Core tracts as the reference level, Outer tracts are predicted to have about 21.95 percentage points fewer households without vehicles, holding median income, renter percentage, and educational attainment constant.

Where is the final model wrong?

ggplot(tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = resid_final), color = NA) +

  theme_void() +

       subtitle = "Red = actual higher than predicted",
       fill = "Residual")









Put your two residual maps side by side, or put them next to each other in the rendered document. Did the clusters from Part 2C shrink? Where did they stay?

map_data <- bind_rows(
  tracts %>%
    mutate(
      model = "Baseline model",
      residual = resid_m1
    ),
  tracts %>%
    mutate(
      model = "Final model",
      residual = resid_final
    )
)

  geom_sf(aes(fill = residual), color = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~model, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166ac",
    mid = "grey95",
    high = "#b2182b",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-50, 50)

    title = "Where the models are wrong",
    subtitle = "Red = actual higher than predicted · Blue = lower than predicted",

The final model reduces some of the strongest residuals, with the maximum positive error falling from roughly 40 to 30 percentage points. Some northern and northeastern tracts become lighter, but errors remain spatially clustered around central, western, and southwestern Philadelphia. This suggests that the new spatial features helped, but the model still does not capture every local condition affecting household vehicle access.


Are the biggest misses in the least reliable tracts?

Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.
Read one coefficient twice. Choose a variable in your final model. Give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
What’s still missing? Look at your final residual map. Name one thing about those places you’d want to measure next, and where you might get the data.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

In this analysis, I predicted the percentage of households without a vehicle across Philadelphia Census tracts. The squared City Hall distance helped the most, lowering CV RMSE from 12.46 in the baseline model to 9.76. This suggests that vehicle access changes with distance from the city center in a curved pattern rather than at one constant rate. The final model, which also included burglary density and distance to an Indego station, lowered RMSE slightly further to 9.71. The log transformation of burglary density disappointed me most. Although logging made the distribution appear more balanced, its RMSE was 11.64, slightly worse than the 11.53 produced by raw burglary density. A cleaner-looking distribution therefore did not automatically produce better predictions.
The estimated β̂ for renter percentage is 0.222, holding median income, educational attainment, burglary density, and the spatial variables constant. In ŷ terms, a tract with a renter share one percentage point higher is predicted to have about 0.22 percentage points more households without vehicles, assuming the other variables remain unchanged.
The final residual map shows smaller errors than the baseline map, but errors are still spatially clustered in parts of central, western, and southwestern Philadelphia. One missing feature may be the quality and frequency of public transportation. Indego stations measure bike-share proximity, but they do not represent subway, trolley, or bus service. I would obtain transit-stop locations and service-frequency information from SEPTA’s GTFS data and test whether better transit access explains the remaining clusters.
Finally, the uncertainty plot shows that prediction errors gradually increase at higher outcome CV values, although only a few tracts have extremely high CVs. Large errors also appear among tracts with relatively reliable estimates. Therefore, ACS uncertainty likely explains part of the remaining error, but the model is also missing neighborhood characteristics that influence whether households own vehicles.
